To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

correlated cognitive change in older people is partly attributable to model specification error and the aggregation of multiple subgroups and that correlated change is more likely to reflect causal commonality in people with preclinical dementia than in healthy older adults.
correlated cognitive change in older individuals may either signify commonality of underlying processes or the cumulative effects multiple age-related conditions.
(a) correlated cognitive change is not necessarily a sign of a single underlying process, and (b) the degree of commonality in cognitive change is related to the degree of dementia in a sample.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new theory of the aging brain that is based on the idea that age-related changes are the result of the accumulation of a large number of small, independent events.
the nature of the relationship between cognitive change in older individuals with and without pre-clinical dementia.
the question of whether the observed correlations among cognitive age-related effects are attributable to common causal processes or to multiple causal factors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
correlated cognitive change is a function of both causal and noncausal processes.

the cognitive age effects observed in older adults are partly attributable to a single underlying causal factor and partly attributable to multiple causal processes. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2019 APA, all rights reserved)

correlated cognitive aging is a function of the aggregation of heterogeneous individuals with multiple age-related conditions, coupled cognitive aging is a feature of the progression to dementia, and the common factor aging theory may be a reasonable approximation in some cases but not others.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
common factor theories of cognitive aging may not be applicable to all cognitive systems and/or that they may be applicable to cognitive systems only in the presence of preclinical dementia.

correlated cognitive change in older adulthood is partly due to a single underlying causal aging process and partly due to multiple heterogeneous age-related conditions that affect multiple cognitive systems.
common factors may be more important in understanding cognitive change in individuals with dementia than in those who are cognitively intact.
The main takeaway from our work is that
correlated cognitive change does not automatically imply commonality of cause.
correlated cognitive change is not necessarily a signature of causal commonality. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2018 APA, all rights reserved)
the common factor aging theory is not a useful framework for explaining correlated cognitive change in older individuals.
